title: Hidden “In-Between” Materials May Aid Batteries and Solar Fuels
summary:
When chemists heat ingredients to make a solid material, they usually focus on the finished product. A new study says the brief stages in the middle can matter just as much.

Researchers reported in Nature Communications that they watched specially designed starter molecules, called single-source precursors, change as temperature rose. By capturing those temporary forms, they found previously unknown material phases that normal methods can miss.

Dr. Sebastian Pike of the University of Warwick said scientists often think only about going from A to B. This work shows many interesting steps between A and B, and some of those hidden steps may be useful on their own.

One discovery was a new, kinetically stabilized form of bismuth vanadate, named β-BiVO4. Ordinary BiVO4 is already studied for clean energy because its band gap—the energy needed to absorb sunlight and drive reactions—helps it use light to help split water and make hydrogen fuel. The new β form has a different atomic arrangement and a larger band gap, so it interacts with light differently. That could give engineers new options for solar fuels, catalysts, and electronics.

Another intermediate found in the experiments could store large amounts of lithium, which raises interest for future batteries. Dr. Dominik Kubicki of the University of Birmingham said these in-between materials are not only stepping stones; they can have useful properties themselves.

The team used tools such as solid-state NMR spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction, and pair distribution function analysis to see structures that usually appear only briefly. They also found that the starting precursor and how it breaks apart strongly affect which materials form.

Pike said studying only a few precursors already suggests a wider chance to find more hidden but useful materials by carefully controlling heat and chemistry.
why_it_matters: Clean energy and better batteries depend on discovering materials that work well with light and charged particles. Looking at temporary stages gives scientists more places to find helpful inventions.
